title: MDCAT Syllabus 2026 — Complete Breakdown by Subject
excerpt: A subject-by-subject look at the MDCAT 2026 syllabus — how the paper is split across Biology, Chemistry, Physics, English, and Logical Reasoning, and what that means for how you divide your study time.

content.text: Start with the syllabus document, not a blog post

Before anything else: the actual syllabus you're preparing from is the PMDC Uniform Curriculum for MDCAT, published on the PMDC website. That document is the only source that matters when there's a disagreement between what an academy tells you and what's officially listed. Download it, keep it open next to your FSc textbooks, and treat every other resource — including this post — as a way to organize that information, not replace it.

PMDC has carried the same syllabus forward for MDCAT 2026 without a fresh overhaul, so if you already have last year's version, you're not starting from zero. Still, check the syllabus section on the official site yourself before you finalize a study plan, since PMDC has said it will communicate any changes directly to candidates.
How the 180 questions are split
MDCAT is a single paper of 180 MCQs, and the five subjects don't get equal weight. Roughly, the split is:

items: Biology — the largest share, close to 45% of the paper
Chemistry — the second-largest, around a quarter of the paper
Physics — a bit less than Chemistry
Logical Reasoning — a small section, similar in size to English

content.text: These percentages are consistent across the major test-prep sources this year, but the exact question count per subject can shift slightly between test cycles. Confirm the current split against the official PMDC syllabus document before you build a subject-by-subject time budget.
The practical takeaway: Biology alone is worth almost as much as Chemistry and Physics combined. If you're deciding where an extra hour of revision goes tonight, that's the math to keep in mind.
Biology: the section that decides your score

Biology carries the most weight, and it's also the subject FSc Pre-Medical students tend to feel most confident about — which is exactly why it's dangerous to under-prepare. A few points dropped here are harder to make up elsewhere.
The syllabus draws from your FSc Biology books across both years, with recurring heavy areas including:

items: Human physiology (support and movement, circulation, respiration, and reproduction)

content.text: Don't assume "I did well in this chapter in my FSc exam" means you're MDCAT-ready on it. Board exams and MDCAT test the same content at different depths — MDCAT leans more on application and comparison-style MCQs than straight recall.
Chemistry: don't let Organic eat all your time

Chemistry splits roughly into Physical, Organic, and Inorganic portions. Physical Chemistry (mole concept, equilibrium, thermochemistry) tends to have a lot of numerical problems, which take longer per question than students expect going in. Organic Chemistry has a reputation for being the hardest to retain, simply because there's more to memorize — reaction mechanisms, functional groups, and nomenclature.

A common mistake: spending disproportionate time perfecting Organic reactions while Physical Chemistry numericals, which are more formulaic and faster to master with practice, get left for "later." Since both carry real weight in the paper, that trade-off usually isn't worth it.
Physics: expect it to feel different from your FSc paper

MDCAT Physics draws from the same FSc syllabus you've studied, but the way it's tested — conceptual, comparison-based MCQs rather than long numerical derivations — can feel unfamiliar the first time you sit a full-length mock. If Physics has been your strongest FSc subject on paper, it's worth testing that assumption early with timed MCQ practice rather than assuming it will transfer automatically.
English and Logical Reasoning: small sections, easy marks

English and Logical Reasoning together make up a small slice of the paper, but they're often the fastest marks available if you prepare for them at all — many students skip practicing this section entirely and lose points that had nothing to do with subject knowledge.

items: English typically covers grammar, vocabulary, and comprehension at a level consistent with FSc English
Logical Reasoning tests pattern recognition, basic quantitative reasoning, and analytical thinking rather than subject content

content.text: Because these sections don't require the same depth of preparation as Biology, Chemistry, or Physics, even a modest, consistent amount of practice — a set of MCQs a few times a week — can lock in marks that are otherwise easy to leave on the table.
Building your study time around the weightage

Once you know how the paper is split, the obvious next step is matching your study calendar to it — not by chapter count, but by how much of the final score each subject controls. If you're building a week-by-week plan, allocate time roughly in proportion to each subject's share of the paper, then adjust based on which chapters you personally find weakest, not which ones feel most comfortable to revise.

If you want a clearer sense of where you currently stand against the aggregate needed for specific colleges, our merit calculator can give you an estimate to work backward from as you plan your remaining months.

Always cross-check subject weightage, exact question counts, and any syllabus updates against the current PMDC Uniform Curriculum document before finalizing your study schedule — test structures have been known to shift slightly between announcement and exam day.
The bottom line

The MDCAT syllabus isn't a mystery — it's public, it's the same FSc content you've already been taught, and the weightage is known in advance. The advantage goes to students who plan around that structure deliberately instead of studying whatever chapter feels most urgent that day. Start with Biology and Chemistry as your foundation, don't neglect Physics just because it's tested differently than you expect, and don't skip English and Logical Reasoning just because they're a smaller share of the paper.

items.question: How is the MDCAT 2026 paper split by subject?
items.answer: 180 MCQs total, split roughly as Biology (~45%, the largest share), Chemistry (~25%), Physics (slightly less than Chemistry), and English and Logical Reasoning as smaller, similarly-sized sections. Confirm the exact current split against the official PMDC syllabus document.

items.question: Which subject should I prioritize most for MDCAT?
items.answer: Biology, since it carries the largest single share of the paper — close to as much as Chemistry and Physics combined. It's also the subject FSc Pre-Medical students tend to feel most confident about, which makes under-preparing for it a common and costly mistake.

items.question: Does doing well in FSc Biology mean I'm ready for MDCAT Biology?
items.answer: Not automatically. Board exams and MDCAT test the same content at different depths — MDCAT leans more on application and comparison-style MCQs than the straight recall that often works for board exams.

items.question: Should I spend more time on Organic or Physical Chemistry?
items.answer: Both carry real weight, so favoring one isn't a good trade. Physical Chemistry numericals are more formulaic and faster to master with practice, while Organic Chemistry takes more raw memorization — neglecting either leaves marks on the table.

items.question: Are English and Logical Reasoning worth preparing for on MDCAT?
items.answer: Yes — even though they're smaller sections, many students skip practicing them entirely and lose easy marks as a result. A modest, consistent amount of practice can lock in points that don't require the same depth as Biology, Chemistry, or Physics.
